name: Chitrey
tagline: A gompa and white chorten at the top of the first climb
meta_description: Chitrey on the Sandakphu trek: the steep first climb from Maneybhanjan, the small monastery and chorten, tea stops, lodges and costs.
summary: Chitrey is the first stop on the Singalila trail, about 3 km and 1.5–2 hours of steep climbing above Maneybhanjan. A small Buddhist gompa and a white chorten stand on the ridge with views back over Darjeeling's hills. Most trekkers stop for tea and walk on to Tumling; a few lodges let you sleep here.

local_story.title: The first prayer flags on the ridge
paras: For travellers heading up the Singalila Ridge, Chitrey has long been the place to catch breath after the hardest hour of the first day. The small Buddhist monastery and the whitewashed chorten beside the trail were built by the Buddhist families of the ridge, Sherpa, Tamang and others, who settled these slopes as herders and farmers. Guides still stop here to turn the prayer wheels and add a khada scarf for a safe trek, a habit many trekkers copy.

The trail from Maneybhanjan to Chitrey was once the only way up; the Land Rover track came later and loops in long bends around it. Walking it, you climb through the edge of the Singalila reserve forest, the tract the British bought from the Sikkim Durbar in 1882. Look back from the chorten on a clear morning and the ridges of Ghoom, Sukhiapokhri and Darjeeling roll away eastward.

did_you_know: The walking trail from Maneybhanjan to Chitrey climbs roughly 400 m in about 3 km, the steepest sustained climb of the first day of the Sandakphu trek.
Just beyond Chitrey, the hamlet of Meghma (about 2,600 m) has a monastery that local accounts date to the early 1950s.
The forest around Chitrey is the first band of red tree rhododendron (Rhododendron arboreum) on the trek, usually flowering in March and April.
intro: Chitrey is less a village than a saddle with a gompa, a chorten, a few houses and a couple of tea shops. You reach it sweating from the climb out of Maneybhanjan, put your pack down on a bench, and look back over the valley you just came up. On clear days the view east reaches the Darjeeling ridge, and in April the slopes around the trail are red with rhododendron.

Most trekkers stop for 20–30 minutes, drink tea and walk on toward Meghma and Tumling, another 7–8 km. But if you started late from Darjeeling, Chitrey is a sensible first night: you have done the steepest part, the lodges are quiet and cheap, and you will reach Tumling the next morning with plenty of time to watch Kanchenjunga.
facts: Small gompa, white chorten, first big climb
costs: Dinner and breakfast at a lodge
Usually priced as part of a longer trip

highlights.title: The gompa and chorten
highlights.text: A small Buddhist monastery and a white chorten sit beside the trail at the top of the climb, strung with prayer flags. Walk clockwise around the chorten, turn the wheels and, if the gompa is open, step in quietly to see the altar. A small donation is welcome.

highlights.title: View back to Darjeeling
highlights.text: From the saddle the ridges of Ghoom, Sukhiapokhri and Darjeeling spread out to the east, with tea gardens and pine forest below. Morning light is best. It is a good place to see how far you have come in under two hours.

highlights.title: Rhododendron forest
highlights.text: The trail from Maneybhanjan to Chitrey passes through the first of the trek's rhododendron and oak forest. In late March and April the red tree rhododendrons flower here before the higher ridge, so even a short walk up from Maneybhanjan gives you blossom.

highlights.title: A gentle path on to Meghma
highlights.text: After Chitrey the trail eases, running past the hamlet of Lamaydhura to Meghma at about 2,600 m, where a monastery and a few houses sit in the cloud. It is a pleasant 1.5–2 hours of mostly level walking before the final climb to Tumling.

highlights.title: A quiet first night
highlights.text: Few trekkers sleep at Chitrey, so its lodges are quiet. If you started late, a night here breaks the first day well and gives you an unhurried sunrise walk to Tumling for the Kanchenjunga view the next morning.

how_to_reach.text: From Maneybhanjan, the trail leaves the end of the bazaar and climbs steeply on stone steps and earth paths for about 3 km. Allow 1.5–2 hours with stops. Your licensed guide must be with you from here, as you are entering the park area.

The Land Rover track from Maneybhanjan passes near Chitrey in about 20–30 minutes, but drivers rarely sell short drops on their own. Ask at the association if you only want a lift here; it is usually priced as part of a trip to Tumling or Sandakphu.

where_to_stay: Chitrey has a couple of small family lodges with basic rooms or dorm beds, thick quilts and simple dinners of dal-bhat or noodles, at roughly ₹400–700 per person for the bed. Toilets are shared and hot water costs extra. Most trekkers prefer to push on to Tumling, 7–8 km further, where there are more lodges and the mountain view. Sleep at Chitrey only if you started after midday or want a short first day.
tips: Start the climb from Maneybhanjan before 10 am; the stone steps are hot and slow in the midday sun.
Take the steepest stretch slowly and keep your heart rate down; it sets your pace for the trek.
Use the Chitrey toilets and refill water; the next tea stop is at Meghma, about 1.5 hours on.
Walk clockwise around the chorten and do not sit on its base.
In April, carry a light raincoat; afternoon showers are common even in flowering season.

experiences.title: Turn the prayer wheels at Chitrey gompa
experiences.summary: Stop at the small monastery and white chorten on the saddle at Chitrey, turn the prayer wheels with your guide and take a few quiet minutes before the ridge proper begins. It is a short pause most trekkers rush past.
body: The chorten at Chitrey is the first big Buddhist monument on the Singalila trail, a whitewashed dome and spire with prayer flags radiating out to the trees. Guides from Maneybhanjan, many of them from Buddhist Sherpa and Tamang families, often stop here to walk around it, touch their foreheads to the base and spin the wheels for a safe journey.

Walk around clockwise, keeping the chorten on your right. If the gompa door is open, take off your shoes and step in quietly; there is usually a simple altar with butter lamps, images of the Buddha and Guru Rinpoche, and offering bowls of water. Photographs inside are best avoided unless someone tells you otherwise.

A small donation in the box helps with the upkeep of a building that sees thousands of trekkers each year. Then sit on the bench outside for ten minutes with a cup of tea. Below you, the trail you climbed winds back down toward the roofs of Maneybhanjan.

faqs.q: Is Chitrey monastery open to visitors?
faqs.a: Usually, yes, though there is no fixed timetable and the door may be locked when the caretaker is away. Trekkers can always walk around the chorten and turn the outer prayer wheels. Remove shoes before entering, walk clockwise and keep your voice low.

faqs.q: Can I photograph Chitrey chorten?
faqs.a: Yes, photographs of the chorten, flags and view are fine. Inside the gompa, ask first, and avoid flash. If people are praying, wait until they finish. The prayer flags look best with morning light from the east.

faqs.q: How long should I stop at Chitrey?
faqs.a: Twenty to thirty minutes is enough for tea, a walk round the chorten and a breather after the climb. If you are staying the night, there is time to walk down a little way into the rhododendron forest in the late afternoon.

experiences.title: The steep first climb from Maneybhanjan
experiences.summary: The 3 km walk from Maneybhanjan to Chitrey is the hardest hour of the first day: about 400 m of climbing on stone steps and earth paths through oak and rhododendron. Do it early and slowly and the rest of the day feels easy.
body: The trail leaves the top of Maneybhanjan's bazaar and almost at once starts to climb, cutting across the bends of the Land Rover track. The path is part stone steps, part earth and roots, steep enough that you will want short steps and regular stops. Forest closes in quickly: oak, chestnut, rhododendron and, higher up, the first moss-hung trees.

Do not race. Your guide has walked this a hundred times and will set a steady pace; keep to it. On the bends where the trail meets the jeep track, step off the road for Land Rovers, which come down fast. Drink water at each stop, and peel off a layer as soon as you warm up.

In late March and April the red flowers of the tree rhododendron light up the forest. In autumn the light is clear and the view behind you opens with every bend. After 1.5–2 hours the gradient eases, prayer flags appear, and you walk out onto the saddle at Chitrey and its white chorten.

faqs.q: How hard is the walk from Maneybhanjan to Chitrey?
faqs.a: It is short but steep: about 3 km and 400 m of climbing, taking 1.5–2 hours. Fit walkers find it tiring rather than difficult. Take it slowly, drink water and use poles if your knees are weak. After Chitrey the trail to Meghma is much gentler.

faqs.q: Can I skip the climb to Chitrey by Land Rover?
faqs.a: Yes, by taking a Land Rover to Tumling or further, but individual drops to Chitrey are rarely sold. Some trekkers ride to Tumling on day one and start walking from there. You lose the first forest section but save energy for the ridge.

faqs.q: Is the Chitrey trail slippery?
faqs.a: In wet weather and in winter frost, yes. The stone steps and roots get slick, especially coming down. Wear boots with good grip. In the monsoon the park is closed; in September and early October expect mud and a few leeches in the lower forest.

experiences.title: Walk on to Meghma and its cloud monastery
experiences.summary: From Chitrey the trail runs gently past Lamaydhura to Meghma, a hamlet at about 2,600 m that is in cloud more often than not, with a monastery that local accounts date to the early 1950s. Tea at Meghma and a look inside the gompa make a good lunch stop.
body: After the steep start, the path from Chitrey to Meghma is a relief: about 3–4 km of rolling trail and jeep track, passing a few farmhouses and the hamlet of Lamaydhura, where tea shops sell noodles and boiled eggs. Fields of potato and cabbage alternate with patches of forest, and on clear days the ridge ahead shows the way to Tonglu.

Meghma's name is often linked to megh, cloud, and it lives up to it: mist often drifts through by late morning. The monastery here is the most substantial on the lower trail, and local accounts say it dates from the early 1950s and holds a large number of Buddha images. There is also an SSB border post; keep your ID handy.

From Meghma the trail splits. The left fork climbs to Tonglu and its trekkers' hut; the right goes to Tumling in Nepal. Your guide will choose based on where you are sleeping. Either way, it is about 1–1.5 hours more, and the gompa is a good place to pause first.

faqs.q: How far is Meghma from Chitrey?
faqs.a: About 3–4 km, usually 1.5–2 hours on foot along a gentle path and parts of the jeep track. From Meghma it is another 1–1.5 hours to Tumling or to Tonglu. Meghma has tea shops and is a natural lunch stop on the first day.

faqs.q: Is there a monastery at Meghma?
faqs.a: Yes. Meghma has a Buddhist monastery that local accounts date to the early 1950s, larger than the gompa at Chitrey. It is usually open in the daytime. Remove shoes, walk clockwise and ask before taking photographs inside.

faqs.q: Do I need ID at Meghma?
faqs.a: Yes, there is an SSB border post at Meghma and staff may check names and ID. Indians should carry a passport or voter ID; foreigners need their passport with an Indian visa. Keep them in an easy pocket rather than at the bottom of your pack.

experiences.title: Dawn over the Darjeeling hills from Chitrey
experiences.summary: If you sleep at Chitrey, get up before dawn and walk to the chorten. The sun rises over the eastern ridges of Darjeeling and Sukhiapokhri, lighting the valleys from above, and the first trekkers will not arrive for hours.
body: Chitrey faces east over the deep valley that separates the Singalila Ridge from the Darjeeling hills. Before sunrise the ridges stack up in shades of blue, with cloud sitting in the valley bottoms in autumn. As the sun clears the hills, the light runs across the slopes toward you and the prayer flags begin to glow.

This is not the Kanchenjunga view, which waits higher at Tumling and Tonglu, but it is quieter and closer to village life. Smoke rises from kitchen fires below, a few cows start for the grazing, and the first Land Rovers of the day can be heard grinding up the track from Maneybhanjan.

Bring a warm jacket; Chitrey can drop to near freezing in December. Watch from the chorten or from the lodge garden, then eat breakfast and set off before the day trekkers come up. You will have the trail to Meghma almost to yourself.

faqs.q: Can you see Kanchenjunga from Chitrey?
faqs.a: Not well; the main view from Chitrey is east over the Darjeeling hills. Kanchenjunga becomes visible higher up, from around Meghma and especially from Tumling and Tonglu. Sleep at Tumling if a sunrise mountain view is your priority.

faqs.q: What time is sunrise at Chitrey?
faqs.a: Roughly 5.15–6.15 am depending on the month: earliest in May and June, latest in December and January. Be at the chorten 20 minutes before for the best colour. Your lodge host can tell you the day's time.

faqs.q: Is it cold at Chitrey at dawn?
faqs.a: In November to February, dawn temperatures are around 0–5 °C, sometimes below. In April and May mornings are mild, 8–12 °C. A down or fleece jacket, cap and gloves are enough for a short sunrise wait.

faqs.q: Where is Chitrey on the Sandakphu trek?
faqs.a: Chitrey is the first stop above Maneybhanjan, about 3 km and 1.5–2 hours up the walking trail. It sits on a saddle with a gompa and chorten. From here the trail continues to Meghma and then to Tumling or Tonglu, the usual first-night stops.

faqs.q: Should I stay overnight at Chitrey?
faqs.a: Only if you started late or want a gentle first day. Most trekkers walk on to Tumling, about 7–8 km further, for its lodges and the Kanchenjunga view. Chitrey's few lodges are basic but quiet and cheaper than Tumling.

faqs.q: Is Chitrey in India or Nepal?
faqs.a: Chitrey is on the Indian side of the border, in Darjeeling district. The trail goes into Nepal later, at Tumling and Jaubari. Carry ID regardless, as there are SSB posts along the way, starting from Meghma.

faqs.q: Can I reach Chitrey by car?
faqs.a: Only by the Land Rover track from Maneybhanjan, which passes near it. Ordinary cars and SUVs from Darjeeling do not go up the Singalila track. Land Rover drops to Chitrey alone are uncommon; it is normally a 1.5–2 hour walk.

faqs.q: Is there food at Chitrey?
faqs.a: Yes, tea shops and lodges sell tea, noodle soup, chowmein, eggs and sometimes momos. A tea costs ₹30–50 and a plate of noodles ₹100–150. Lunch on the first day is usually at Chitrey or Meghma.

faqs.q: Does Chitrey have mobile network?
faqs.a: Indian networks usually work at Chitrey because it faces Darjeeling. Signal becomes patchier toward Tumling, where Nepali networks take over in places. Make any important calls here or in Maneybhanjan.

faqs.q: When do rhododendrons bloom at Chitrey?
faqs.a: The lower forest around Chitrey usually flowers in late March and April, a couple of weeks ahead of the higher ridge. Red tree rhododendron comes first. Bloom timing varies with the winter, so ask your guide or check recent trekker reports.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide to walk to Chitrey?
faqs.a: Yes. The guide requirement applies from the start of the trail at Maneybhanjan, and you register before you start. Even a day walk to Chitrey and back is normally done with a guide.

faqs.q: Can I do Chitrey as a day trip from Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Yes. Take an early shared jeep to Maneybhanjan, walk up to Chitrey and Meghma with a guide, and return the same afternoon. It is a good half-day hike with forest and a monastery, though the high mountain views need you to go further.
